name: H5 Data Centers

profile.reading: Per H5 Data Centers own site, this Cleveland, Ohio facility sits at 1625 Rockwell Ave and totals 351,000 square feet, built to Tier III colocation standard with 2N UPS power and 2N backup generators rated for 48 hour diesel runtime. The page does not state a power capacity in MW. The facility offers access to 23 on-net carriers and the CL-IX, FD-IX, and Ohio IX internet exchanges, and is SOC 2, ISO 27001, and PCI-DSS compliant, with a 100 percent sales and use tax abatement under an Ohio incentive program. H5 Data Centers is a privately held US colocation and wholesale data center operator with facilities spanning roughly two dozen markets nationwide, per the company's own site, of which this Cleveland facility is one of its largest publicized builds at 351,000 square feet. Cleveland has drawn colocation and enterprise IT investment in part on the strength of Ohio's state and local data center tax abatement program, which the operator's own page cites directly, offering a 100 percent sales and use tax exemption on qualifying equipment purchases tied to job and investment commitments; this incentive has also drawn hyperscale investment elsewhere in the state, though that broader trend is not attributed to this specific building. H5 markets this facility for its access to 23 on-net carriers and three regional internet exchanges (CL-IX, FD-IX, and Ohio IX), positioning it as a Midwest interconnection point distinct from the coastal markets where H5 also operates. H5 is not a publicly traded company and does not file SEC disclosures, so this entry's power, cooling, and certification details are sourced solely to the operator's own published facility page rather than an independently corroborating source, a limitation this registry notes rather than treats as disqualifying, consistent with its general practice for privately held colocation operators. No year-opened date or third-party audited MW capacity figure was located for this specific address this session.

profile.business_description: National provider of wholesale data centers and colocation services

reading:
H5 Data Centers is a wholesale and colocation operator headquartered in Greenwood Village, Colorado. It was founded in 2010 and is privately held by founder and chief executive Josh Simms with backing from his father Ronald Simms through H5 Capital, L.P., which makes it one of the few operators of its size in this registry with no institutional fund or listed parent behind it. Its growth strategy has been to buy existing buildings with tenants already in them rather than to develop greenfield campuses, and that shows in the character of its portfolio, which the company describes as more than 2.3 million square feet under management across twenty United States markets.

Two of the acquisitions explain the company well. In January 2011 H5 bought 1000 Denny Way in Seattle, a 285,000 square foot building whose principal tenant was and remained The Seattle Times. That is why the registry's Seattle row is still named after the newspaper. The building had long carried carrier presence including Level 3 and XO, and H5's interest was in the interconnection and the shell rather than in a clean sheet. In January 2017 it bought the Cleveland Technology Center on Rockwell Avenue in downtown Cleveland, a 351,000 square foot carrier hotel and enterprise facility, and expanded it by 25,000 square feet in 2018 with most of the new capacity pre leased to a single large tenant and with the project qualifying for Ohio sales and use tax abatement. Then in January 2022 H5 bought seven facilities from vXchnge in Nashville, Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, Portland, Secaucus, St Louis and St Paul, adding about 280,000 square feet and, in the language of the announcement, 20.6 megawatts of generator backup power.

That last figure is worth pausing on, because it is exactly the kind of number that gets reprinted as capacity. Generator backup power is standby generation. It is not critical IT load and it is not the utility service, and 20.6 megawatts spread across seven buildings tells you about resilience design rather than about how much computing those buildings support.

The individual sites in this registry show the same pattern. The Portland facility, one of the vXchnge buildings, is at 1233 NW 12th Avenue, 42,000 square feet, with an N plus one uninterruptible power supply and two megawatts of generator backup with 48 hours of diesel, eight on net carriers and access to the Northwest Access Exchange. The San Antonio facility at 100 Taylor Street is 85,000 square feet across two buildings with 2N uninterruptible power, generator backed utility supply, 48 hours of diesel and about 35 carriers, with a third phase of expansion described. Neither publishes a critical IT figure. The Ashburn building is the exception and is the newest of the group, a 255,000 square foot Tier III facility at 21800 Beaumeade Circle rated at up to 60 MVA with access to 42 megawatts from Dominion, air cooled chillers with outside air economisation and fan walls, 25 foot slab to slab heights and LEED Silver certification, with the first phase available in the third quarter of 2024. Here the 60 MVA is apparent power capacity and the 42 megawatts is utility service from Dominion. Neither is an IT load, and the two should never be quoted interchangeably.

One address note. The Cleveland row in this registry carries 1525 Rockwell Avenue while H5 markets the site as 1625 Rockwell Avenue, and the complex spans a run of addresses along that block, so the two most likely describe the same campus. The Ashburn building also stands a few hundred feet from the Cologix ASH1 and ASH2 buildings recorded separately in this registry, all three on Beaumeade Circle.
